chunks: From him, from Bakr ibn Muhammad and Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr, both, from Fadl ibn Yunus, who said:

Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) had breakfast with me in Mina, and Muhammad ibn Zayd was with him. They were brought sukurrajat (sweets/candies), and in them was rabitha (a type of impurity or unclean substance). Muhammad ibn Zayd said to him, 'This is rabitha.' He said, so he took a morsel, dipped it in it, and then ate it.

key_terms.أَبُو الْحَسَنِ: Abu al-Hasan (Imam al-Rida, peace be upon him)
key_terms.الرَّبِيثَا: A type of impurity or unclean substance found in food

ai.seo_question: Does the presence of impurity in food make it haram to eat according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Rida (peace be upon him) demonstrates the permissibility of consuming food containing a minor impurity (*rabitha*) by dipping a morsel into it and eating it, indicating that its presence does not render the food haram. This act serves as a practical legal precedent (*amali*) for the principle of *istishab* (presumption of continuity of permissibility) when the impurity is not overwhelming or clearly identifiable as a distinct substance, reflecting the Shia juristic approach to minor impurities in consumables.
